premise: Third Era Tamriel, generations before the Camoran Usurper crisis and centuries before the Dagon invasion — a quiet, unremarkable stretch of the Septim Peace. In Larenne, a moorland market town in Glenumbra, High Rock, an Argonian doorsman at a coaching inn goes about an unremarkable life. He does not know what he is. Somewhere under his skin, under memory itself, is a mark the Hist placed on him as a hatchling before he ever left Black Marsh — and something, someday, is going to call it awake.
tone: Quiet dread, weighted deliberately heavy — even ordinary inn scenes should carry a faint undercurrent of wrongness. Daily life at a Breton inn — gossip, coin, small cruelties and kindnesses — with an undercurrent that surfaces gradually: uncanny stillness before violence, dreams of trees that do not grow in High Rock, a discipline the body seems to already know. Folk-horror pacing, not war-epic pacing. Personal stakes, not world-ending ones. Political intrigue is real but secondary to dread; warmth/levity is the minority note.
magic: Ordinary and Breton-flavored on the surface — Direnni-descended hedge magic, innate Breton magic resistance as a known racial fact, temple restoration, the everyday competence of a land that has always lived comfortably alongside magic. Beneath that surface: Hist-communion (utterly outside Breton frameworks, and the PC's own inheritance), the old Argonian assassin-cult discipline of the Shadowscales, and — seeded for later, not soon — the blood-curse of vampirism, present in the region via genuine Iliac Bay clan lore.
setting: A single Breton market town and its moorland surroundings in Glenumbra, High Rock
genre_bend: Hidden-identity folk horror played anthropologically, Le Guin-style: the PC is, unknown to himself, a Shadowscale — an Argonian bred and marked from hatchlinghood by the Hist to serve as one of the Dark Brotherhood's deadliest instruments, called to that service by a summons he has not yet received. The campaign is NOT about racing toward that reveal. It is a slow accumulation of small wrongnesses — a stillness in him that unsettles people, a knife-sense that surprises even him, dreams he doesn't mention to anyone — building toward a moment, far off, when something finally calls him by what he is. A second, optional long-arc thread (vampirism, via the real Iliac Bay clan lore of High Rock) is available to the player later, and should be seeded lightly, not pushed.
art_style: In the style of Flemish tapestry-weaving rendered through the damp, restrained ink-wash palette of a Breton illuminated manuscript
chronicler_name: Brother Aumery of the Larenne Chapterhouse
chronicler_persona: A minor chapterhouse scribe with more curiosity than rank, who illustrates the town's notable happenings in the margins of his ledgers half out of duty and half because he can't help himself. Fussy, gently ironic, prone to moralizing captions he can't resist adding.

axes.bend: One Glenumbra market town (Larenne) and its immediate moorland/coaching-road surroundings, rendered in real load-bearing detail, rather than High Rock sketched thin.

Breton petty nobility and town governance, the inn's own social web, and — hidden beneath — the Dark Brotherhood/Shadowscale thread and a lightly-seeded vampire clan (Iliac Bay lore), neither to be pushed to the foreground early.
The unglamorous middle of the Septim Peace: far enough from any invasion or crisis that daily life, not war, is the texture. Local town history matters more than empire-wide events.

Breton feudal/magical culture as the visible world, Argonian/Hist culture as the submerged, half-remembered counter-culture inside the PC himself — this contrast is the anthropological spine of the whole campaign.

Hist-communion and Shadowscale discipline as folk-horror-adjacent and mostly dormant; Breton hedge-magic as ordinary background; vampirism (real Iliac Bay clan lore) seeded as a distant, optional thread.
Ordinary Glenumbra moorland fauna and hazards, kept sparse — this is not a monster-hunting campaign.
